city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.lede: Yesterday's high of 51°F was typical for November 13.
text.p_yest: The high of 51°F was typical for November 13. The normal high for the date is 56°F, and the record is 74°F (1902). The low of 41°F was typical for November 13.
text.t_rec: Record highs keep coming. Record lows have nearly stopped.
text.p_rec: If Philadelphia's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Philadelphia has set 7 standing record lows, far fewer than the 64 that chance alone would give, and 100 record highs, far more than the 64 that chance alone would give. The 1990s hold the most record highs of any decade (42). Philadelphia's all-time high is 106°F, on August 7, 1918.
text.t_chg: Philadelphia's days and nights both warmed. Days warmed faster.
text.p_chg: Across 152 complete years: Philadelphia's average low has risen +0.11°F per decade (95% range +0.05 to +0.17), about +1.7°F since 1874. Philadelphia's average high has risen +0.27°F per decade (95% range +0.23 to +0.32), about +4.1°F since 1874.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in 6 of 12 months. Highs rose in 11 of 12 months.
text.t_rain: Rain and snow: no clear long-term change
text.p_rain: Philadelphia's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (+0.21 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 44.1 inches a year. The wettest year was 2011 (64.33 in); the driest, 1922 (29.31 in).
